title: Kansas City BBQ Sauce
subtitle: Sweet, thick tomato-and-molasses barbecue sauce
excerpt: Kansas City BBQ sauce is the thick, sweet, deeply coloured sauce that most people picture when they think of American barbecue. Built on ketchup, molasses, and brown sugar, it's rich, slightly smoky, and coats whatever it's brushed onto.
sourceNotes: Kansas City-style barbecue sauce is the commercial standard in American barbecue. This is a from-scratch version following the classic tomato-molasses structure.

recipe.batchNotes: Make a double or triple batch and keep in sterilised jars in the fridge for up to three weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps in the fridge for three weeks. The flavour deepens after a day.

content.text: Kansas City BBQ sauce is built on ketchup and molasses: thick, sweet, dark, and slightly smoky. It goes on ribs, brisket, pulled pork, and chicken in the final minutes of cooking to caramelise to a lacquered finish. The recipe takes fifteen minutes and the result is significantly better than anything from a bottle.
Combine all the ingredients in a small saucepan and stir until mixed.
Stir over medium heat until combined. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook, stirring often, for 12 to 15 minutes until the sauce thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon.
Taste and adjust: more vinegar if it needs sharpening, more molasses if it needs depth, more cayenne if it needs heat. Pour into a sterilised jar and cool before refrigerating.

items.symptom: The sauce is very thick and stiff
items.fix: Add a splash of water or apple juice and stir over low heat to loosen. The sauce thickens further when it cools, so pull it from the heat while still a little looser than you want.

items.symptom: The sauce tastes one-dimensional and very sweet
items.cause: The balance between sweet and sour is off.
items.fix: Add another tablespoon of cider vinegar and a pinch of salt. The sauce needs the vinegar to stop it tasting like ketchup with sugar.

items.symptom: The sauce has a slightly burned smell
items.cause: Sugar can scorch on the base of the pan.
items.fix: Keep stirring throughout and use a medium rather than high heat. If the base starts to stick, lower the heat immediately.

items.symptom: The sauce splits and looks oily
items.cause: Not possible with this recipe as there's no added fat.
items.fix: If there's a sheen on the surface, it's likely the ketchup's natural oils. Stir well and it will reincorporate.

content.text: KC-style sauce became the dominant commercial BBQ sauce from the mid-20th century. Brands like KC Masterpiece spread the thick, sweet, tomato-and-treacle profile across America. The homemade version has more going on: the smoked paprika adds a genuine smokiness, and the mustard powder gives it a subtle background heat. Use it for basting ribs, as a dipping sauce, on burgers, or as a base for barbecue chicken.
